sourceLesson: Backend LLD: Pythonic-2: Collections, Dataclasses, Type Hints and Exceptions

questions.title: Why Use Dataclass?
questions.question: What is the main benefit of using @dataclass on a class instead of writing it manually?

options.optionText: It automatically generates methods like __init__, __repr__, and __eq__ based on the fields you declare
It automatically makes the class run faster than a normal class
It automatically converts the class into a dictionary
It prevents the class from ever being used inside a list

questions.title: Frozen Dataclass Behavior
questions.question:
Consider the following code snippet:

```python
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Point:
    x: int
    y: int

p = Point(2, 3)
p.x = 10
print(p.x)
```

What happens when this code runs?

options.optionText: It prints 10
It raises a FrozenInstanceError
It prints 2
It raises a TypeError at class definition itself

questions.title: Debugging Mutable Default Trap
questions.question:
A student tries to give every Member object an empty list of borrowed books:
```python
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class Member:
    name: str
    books: list = []
```
Running this raises an error. What is the correct fix?

options.optionText: Change list to tuple and keep = []
Remove the type hint list completely
Change books: list = [] to books: list = field(default_factory=list)
Move books above name in the class

questions.title: Choosing the Right Exception Approach
questions.question: You're writing a borrow(book, member) function for a library system. If the book isn't available, you want the caller to know exactly why it failed (not just get a False or a generic error) and be able to catch that specific failure separately from other library errors. What's the best approach?

options.optionText: Raise a custom exception like BookNotAvailable that inherits from a base LibraryError class
Return False from the function when the book isn't available
Print an error message and return None
Use a bare except: block inside borrow() to silently ignore the problem

questions.title: Enum Usage and Value Extraction
questions.question:
Consider the following code snippet:

```python
from enum import Enum

class LoanStatus(Enum):
    ACTIVE = "active"
    RETURNED = "returned"

status = LoanStatus.ACTIVE
print(status.value)
```

What is printed?

options.optionText: LoanStatus.ACTIVE
active
ACTIVE
It raises an AttributeError

questions.title: Writing the Student Class Cleanly
questions.question: You need to create a Student class with name and marks attributes for the sorting problem. You want it to have __init__, __repr__, and __eq__ automatically, without typing them by hand. Which approach is correct?

options.optionText: Write __init__, __repr__, and __eq__ yourself inside the class
Store each student as a plain dict like {"name": ..., "marks": ...}
Use a namedtuple, since it also updates marks easily after creation
Use @dataclass and declare name: str and marks: int as the fields

questions.title: Defaultdict Behavior
questions.question:
Consider the following code snippet:
```python
from collections import defaultdict

groups = defaultdict(list)
groups["a"].append(1)
groups["a"].append(2)
groups["b"].append(3)

print(groups["c"])
```
What gets printed?

options.optionText: KeyError
None

questions.title: Debug Group Anagrams Logic

options.optionText: The key should be sorted(word) converted to a string, so that anagrams map to the same key
The bug is using a dict — a list should be used instead
The bug is in groups[key].append(word) — it should be groups[key] = word
There is no bug; the code is correct as is

questions.title: Choosing the Right Tool for Frequency Count
questions.question: You need to count how many times each word appears in a large paragraph, and then quickly find the 3 most frequent words. Which tool is the most convenient choice?

options.optionText: deque
namedtuple
Counter from collections
A plain list with nested loops

questions.title: Generic Compare Function Output
questions.question:
Consider the following code snippet:
```python
def compare(x, y, key=None):
    if key:
        x, y = key(x), key(y)
    if x < y:
        return -1
    elif x > y:
        return 1
    return 0

result = compare(5, 3)
print(result)
```
What does this print?

options.optionText: True
